chunks: "The basic equation is P equals VI : power equals voltage times current.
It makes sense dimensionally: voltage is energy per unit charge and current is charge per second, so their product is energy per second, which is watts.
For a resistor I can substitute Ohm's law to get P equals I to the 2R or P equals V squared over R . I pick whichever uses what I know.
If I know the current through a sense resistor, I to the 2R is easiest; if I know the voltage across a resistor, V squared over R .
So 12 volts across 1 kilohms is 144 milliwatts, which is already more than an 0603 resistor is rated for.
For AC, the instantaneous power is still v(t) times i(t) , but what matters is the average, which is V rmsI rms cosine , where is the phase between voltage and current.
For a pure resistor cosine equals 1 ; for a pure capacitor or inductor the average is zero.
In practice I use it constantly: checking resistor wattage, working out that an LDO going from 5 to 3. 3 volts at half an amp burns 0.
85 watts, or estimating battery life from average power."
